newsitem.title: USA: Sheik Abdel-Rahman condemns letter bombs.
newsitem.headline: Sheik Abdel-Rahman condemns letter bombs.

text.p: Sheikhh Omar Abdel-Rahman, the blind cleric convicted of conspiracy in a plot to blow up the United Nations, on Tuesday condemned the recent spate of letter bombs and accused the Egyptian government of sending them, according to his translator and legal aide.
"I condemn these acts," the militant Egyptian preacher said in a telephone call to the translator, Ahmed Sattar, from the federal prison in Springfield, Missouri, where he is serving a life sentence.
"This proves again that this criminal (Cairo) regime is willing to do anything to harm Islamists in the West and ruin the Moslem reputation," he was quoted as saying.

Abdel-Rahman was convicted in 1995 with nine others for conspiracy to bomb the United Nations and other buildings in New York. He was also convicted in connection with a plot to assassinate Eyptian President Hosni Mubarak.
The cleric, who suffers from diabetes, high blood pressure and heart disease, is serving his sentence at the prison's hospital.

He was questioned about the letter bombs sent this month to offices of the Arabic-language newspaper Al-Hayat in London, Riyadh, Washington and most recently, at the United Nations. In London on Monday two security guards were injured.
Abdel-Rahman said he and his followers have the "highest regard" for Al-Hayat, saying "they have published everything we have ever said."
"They have been very fair to us in publishing our viewpoint," he told his translator.

"But it is very obvious to me that the Egyptian government is doing this dirty work because our appeals have recently been filed with the courts in New York and they want to stir things up to show Americans how evil we are," he said.

Sattar said the Sheikhh also reminded him that urea nitrogen was the chemical alleged to have been used in the Feb. 26, 1993 World Trade Centre blast that killed six people and injured more than 1,000 others. Authorities said that the letter bombs contained the plastic explosive Semtex.
The Sheikhh's followers were convicted in the World Trade Centre bombing.

No one has claimed reponsibility for the letter bombs and Al-Hayat journalists have speculated only that it may have come from enemies of the newspaper's coverage of the Middle East. The letter bombs sent to Washington and the United Nations all bore an Alexandria, Egypt postmark and a Dec. 21 date.

Three letter bombs also turned up in the areas around Leavenworth federal prison in Kansas, which houses Mohammad Salameh, a militant Moslem jailed for life for the World Trade Centre bombing, and Victor Alvarez and Mohammed Saleh, convicted of plotting to blow up U.N. headquarters.

Al-Hayat is owned by Prince Khaled bin Sultan, son of Saudi Arabia's powerful Defence Minister Prince Sultan and a nephew of King Fahd. The Saudi royal family has been condemned by Moslem militants for its tight alliance with Washington.

The newspaper has in the past been temporarily banned in Saudi Arabia and other Arab states where official publications devote much coverage to praising leaders and their activities. It has allowed militants to air their views.
